overview: This two-document file concerns Japanese harbor development in colonial Taiwan and its relationship to Japan’s southward expansion. A 1938 cross-reference sheet directs researchers to a report from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on the strategic significance of the Port of Takao, including material derived from the Italian naval attaché in Tokyo. A 1939 consular despatch from Taipei reports that the new port at Gosei in Taichu Province had officially been named Niitaka and describes its christening by Governor-General Kobayashi before government and business representatives.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on the Port of Takao and Japan’s “Southward Advance”
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to a report on the significance of the Port of Takao for Japan’s “Southward Advance” policy.
subfiles.summary: This filing sheet cross-references document no. 3039 from Grew in Japan to decimal file 794.00/131. The referenced report assessed the Port of Takao in Formosa in relation to Japan’s southward policy. It reportedly enclosed a U.S. naval attaché’s report containing a translation of information sent to the Italian Admiralty by the Italian naval attaché in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the naming of Niitaka Harbor
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Emmerson reports the official naming and christening of the new harbor at Gosei as Niitaka.
subfiles.summary: Emmerson refers to earlier consular reports concerning the planned port at Gosei and the industrialization of Taiwan. He reports that the harbor had officially been named “Niitaka Ko,” or “Port of Niitaka.” Governor-General Kobayashi christened it on September 25 at a ceremony attended by more than 800 government officials, local governors, and prominent businessmen.

interest: The file links civilian infrastructure development in colonial Taiwan with wider assessments of Japanese strategic expansion toward Southeast Asia. It is especially useful because it juxtaposes international naval-intelligence reporting about Takao with a routine consular account of the ceremonial naming of a new port. The attendance of more than 800 officials and businessmen at the Niitaka ceremony also illustrates the close connection between colonial administration, local government, and commercial interests in Taiwan’s late-1930s industrial development.
